Standing tall and commanding, Carla approaches Julian with a piercing gaze. She extends her arm for a firm handshake. "I'm Carla. I'll be your bodyguard both inside the Redmist Estate and wherever else you go. You'll notice me around frequently, so don't try to shake me off." She steps back, crossing her arms. "I need you to understand that your safety is my top priority. Everything I do is to keep you safe. Let's work together to make sure nothing compromises that. Firstly, I'll ask to borrow your phone. It won't take long."

[#1330 Julian]
Julian met her handshake firmly, matching her gaze. "Phone's in my pocket," he said, fishing it out and handing it over. "Mind if I ask what for?" He kept his tone easy, but his eyes stayed on her, studying the way she handled it. "I'm not in the habit of handing my things over without knowing why — even to someone charged with keeping me alive."

[#1331 Narration]
Carla took the phone without ceremony, her thumb already moving across the screen. She flipped it face-down, prised off the back casing with a practiced motion, and slipped a thin metallic disc no larger than a coin beneath the battery. The casing snapped shut.

"Signal relay. Lets me trace it if you go missing." She held it back toward him. "A precaution, nothing more. I put one in Bernard's phone too, and he grumbled about it for the better part of a month."

Her sunglasses came down then, folded and tucked into her breast pocket, revealing the flat blue of her eyes. They didn't soften any.

"Anything else you want to ask before we go through these gates? Because once we're inside, everyone in that house will want something from you, and the questions only get harder."

[#1332 Julian]
Julian turned the phone over in his fingers once, then slid it back into his pocket. "Bernard grumbled about it for a month and kept it in his phone. That tells me something." He tipped his head toward the gates. "Alright. I've got one question, and I'd rather hear it from you than figure it out the hard way. In that house — who's actually on my side?" He glanced at her. "I'm not asking for names to trust. I'm asking who's going to be watching me like a creditor the moment I walk through that door."

[#1333 Narration]
Carla's mouth pulled to one side, mulling it over before the answer came.

"Jezebel. My money's on her — Bernard trusted her with the books for twelve years, and she'll bury you in paperwork before she lets the estate bleed. She's not going to hug you, but her interest and yours run the same direction. Beyond that, Lisette sees everything and says none of it; treat her with respect and she'll be worth more than any advisor." She glanced toward the mansion. "As for the way they'll look at you — the staff see a stranger who inherited their lives. The board members see a woodcutter's son holding a key they spent decades coveting. Then there's the widow." Her pause sat there a moment. "Gabriella spent two years deciding this estate was hers. Try not to let her near your ear alone."

[#1334 Julian]
Julian let out a short breath through his nose, not quite a laugh.

"A woodcutter's son. That's a generous way of putting it." He adjusted the strap of his bag on his shoulder. "So — Jezebel's the one with sense, Lisette's the one with eyes, and Gabriella's the one I keep at arm's length. Simple enough."

He turned toward the gates, then paused, glancing back at Carla.

"One more thing, and then I'll stop stalling. You said heavier threats than Bernard faced. What exactly are we talking about? Because a widow who wants my ear doesn't keep a bodyguard on the payroll."

[#1335 Narration]
Carla rolled her shoulder, as if the question had settled somewhere stiff.

"Bernard was a rich old man with a charitable name. That buys you threats of the quiet sort — blackmail, a lawsuit someone hoped he'd settle, the occasional creditor with a grudge. Manageable." She looked out past the gates, along the street where the harbour fog was thinning in the morning light. "An inheritance this size, contested, with the widow still living under the roof? That's a different animal. People who were patient for twenty years suddenly aren't. I want you alive long enough to find out which of them stops being patient first."

She nodded toward the gatehouse. "Now. Shall we?"

[#1336 Julian]
Julian gave a short nod and stepped toward the gatehouse, his boots crunching on the gravel. "Then let's not keep the patient ones waiting."

He raised his chin as the iron gates began to swing, taking in the mansion beyond — the columns, the long sweep of drive, the figures he could already make out near the doors. His bag sat square on his shoulder. Whatever was waiting in that house, he meant to walk through the front door on his own two feet.

"Woodcutter's son," he muttered, half to himself. "Let's see what he makes of this."

[#1337 Narration]
The gates parted with a low groan of old iron, and the drive unfolded before them — gravel raked into neat furrows, hedges clipped to a hard edge, the mansion's columns pale against a sky the colour of dishwater. Two figures waited near the doors. One was a maid in a black dress and white apron, hands folded, posture immaculate. The other was a woman in a tailored slate suit, a leather folder tucked under her arm, a pen already in her fingers as though she'd been mid-thought and simply carried it outside with her.

Carla walked half a step behind and to Julian's left, her eyes sweeping the upper windows.

"That's Jezebel with the folder," she murmured. "The maid is Lisette."

[#1338 Julian]
Julian closed the last of the gravel between himself and the two women at the doors, and stopped a polite pace short. His eyes went to the folder first, then to its owner.

"You'd be Jezebel, then." He offered his hand. "Julian Redmist. I'm told you kept my grandfather's books straight for twelve years, so I imagine you've got a list in that folder and I'd rather see it sooner than later." A brief flick of his gaze to the maid. "And Lisette. Carla says you see everything and say none of it — I'll try not to give you anything worth talking about on my first morning."

[#1339 Narration]
Jezebel took his hand in a grip that was businesslike rather than warm. "The list would take most of the morning, so I'll spare you the reading and give you the headline. It's not a ledger's worth of problems, it's half a dozen names attached to half a dozen expectations."

Before she could continue, the tall doors swung wide. A blonde swept out into the daylight, unhurried, her purple dress catching the morning like a stage curtain — heels, pearls, a wine-dark shawl draped across her arms as though the weather were her guest. Gabriella stopped at the top of the steps, chin lifted a fraction.

"There you are." Her eyes travelled the gravel drive and landed. "I'd begun to fear the city had swallowed you whole."

[#1340 Julian]
Julian turned from Jezebel toward the steps, and let his gaze travel up the full height of her unhurried once — the shawl, the pearls, the heels that had no business on gravel.

"Swallowed me whole. That's one way to put it." He didn't move to climb the steps. "Your husband's will only found me two weeks ago, so I've had most of that time just getting here." He set his bag down at his feet, deliberately. "You'll be Gabriella, then. I'd rather not start off pretending we don't both know what that makes this — so why don't you tell me what you came out here to say."

[#1341 Narration]
Gabriella descended two steps, unhurried, and let the shawl slip from one shoulder as though the sun had grown too warm for it. "Blunt. You didn't get that from Bernard — he'd have made me wait three days for an answer and called it diplomacy." Her smile stayed fixed. "What I came out to say is that we're both living in this house, sharing a name neither of us chose, and it will go easier for both of us if we're not enemies over a will that's already been read. I know the staff. I know the board. You'll be lost in this house by dinnertime otherwise."

Behind her, Jezebel's pen stopped moving.

[#1342 Julian]
Julian let the silence hang a moment, then picked his bag back up and climbed the steps — not in a hurry, not deferential, just steady.

"You've made the offer sound very generous," he said, stopping a step below her so they were near eye to eye. "Three days of Bernard's diplomacy in my pocket, if I want it."

He glanced past her into the shadow of the entrance hall, then back. "Here's my problem with it. You say the board and the staff — but the will didn't leave me a house full of friends, it left me a house full of people who liked the way things were. So I'll take the help where it's offered honestly. What I won't do is let you be the one who decides which of them gets to reach me." He tipped his head toward Jezebel's folder. "She's holding the list. I'd rather start there."

[#1343 Narration]
Gabriella's jaw shifted a fraction, and for a moment the smile was a thing she wore rather than had. Then she gathered her shawl back over her shoulder with a flick.

"Then I'll leave you to your list." She came down the last steps and passed him, close enough that her perfume trailed behind her like a receipt. "The house is large, Julian. You'll want a friend in it before the week's out."

Jezebel had the folder open before Gabriella cleared the gravel. "Cole Trust, the Carrow bequest, the harbour property lease, two cousins on Bernard's side who believe the will's invalid, and the foundations, which want to know by Friday whether their funding survives the change in management." She closed it again. "That's the whole of it. Welcome to the family business."

[#1344 Julian]
Julian took the folder's edge between his fingers, not pulling it away, just holding it. "Cousins who think the will's invalid and foundations that need an answer by Friday." He exhaled slowly. "I've been in this house four minutes."

He looked from Jezebel to the hallway beyond — the portraits, the swept marble, the quiet wealth of it all pressing in. "Alright. Start me with the foundations, since they apparently can't wait. But I want to know what they do before I decide anything about their money." He let go of the folder and turned toward the entrance hall proper. "And Jezebel — is there somewhere in this house I can sit down and read that isn't a throne room?"

[#1345 Narration]
Jezebel tucked the folder back under her arm and led him past the portraits. "The library. Bernard did his reading there. It's the one room in this house that never learned to show off."

The corridor opened into a long room lined with shelves to the ceiling, a fire already laid in the grate, and a pair of worn armchairs arranged around a low table that looked like it had hosted a great many long arguments. Jezebel set the folder down and drew out a single page, sliding it toward him.

"Three foundations. The widows' fund, the school in the eastern quarter, and the clinic. Bernard funded all three out of his own pocket. The clinic's the one that matters — it's the only surgery on that side of the harbour, and it runs on our money and not much else." She tapped the bottom line. "Their director's expecting an answer on Friday. If the money stops, the doors close inside a month."

[#1346 Julian]
Julian pulled the page closer and read it where he stood, one hand flat on the table. His mouth moved faintly as he worked through the figures.

"Three months of reserve. Less, if the harbour lease doesn't renew — and I notice that's on your list too." He looked up. "Bernard's name is on the clinic door, and you're telling me the director doesn't know if he's got a job on Friday. So let's not keep them dangling." He straightened. "Draw up what the clinic needs to stay open a year. Not a token — what it actually costs. If the numbers hold, I'll sign it before the day's out. And the other two can have the same answer once I've seen them."

He set the page down. "But I want to ride over and see that surgery with my own eyes before I put my name to its money. Carla can come. What else do you need from me before Friday, Jezebel?"

[#1347 Narration]
Jezebel pulled a slim pen from her breast pocket and made two quick marks in the folder's margin. "The clinic's director is called Dr. Osei. He'll want the money and he won't trust you for a moment, because he spent two years sure Bernard was about to change his mind." She glanced up. "And Julian — the cousins have written to the estate three times since the will was read. I've kept the letters. You should read them before they decide you've been ignoring them."

She straightened her suit jacket. "Nothing else. The rest can wait until you've seen the clinic for yourself."

[#1348 Julian]
"Then leave the letters here with me, and I'll read them before I go anywhere." Julian pulled one of the worn armchairs back and sat down, gesturing at the paper still on the table. "And write down Dr. Osei's name for me. I don't intend to walk in there not knowing who I'm talking to."

He glanced toward the window and the papers scattered across Bernard's desk, then back to Jezebel. "One thing before you go. A year of funding for that clinic is easy to promise in a letter. Do you think it's the right number, or is that just what the clinic asked for?"

[#1349 Narration]
Jezebel wrote the name in a neat hand and tore the corner from her notepad. She answered without flinching. "It's the number the clinic asked for and the number I'd have argued for anyway. Bernard cut them to the bone for two years while he fretted over his legacy, and the place has been running on goodwill and unpaid overtime. A year's funding doesn't make it comfortable. It makes it honest."

She slid the slip across the table. "The letters are in the top drawer. I'll leave you to them."

Her heels crossed the library floor, then stopped at the door. "One thing worth knowing about your grandfather. He was right about more things than most men. He was also wrong about the clinic, and he knew it at the end. He just couldn't bring himself to fix it while he still had time." The door clicked softly on its hinge.

[#1350 Julian]
Julian sat with that a moment, the slip of paper between his fingers, then pulled the top drawer open and set the letters out in front of him. He read them slowly, one by one, and when he finished he didn't set them down so much as let them drift to the table.

"The clinic first, then." He turned toward the door. "Carla — fetch Lisette, will you? If I'm riding into the eastern quarter I'd rather know what to expect before I get there, and Jezebel's the only one in this house who's given me a straight answer so far." He picked up the slip with Dr. Osei's name. "Actually, never mind. I'll walk down and find her myself. Stretch my legs, see the house the way Bernard saw it."

[#1351 Narration]
The door had barely shut behind Jezebel when Julian rose, and the corridor beyond the library smelled of beeswax and old stone. He passed a long gallery where Redmist faces watched from frames — surgeons mostly, judging by the instruments in their portraits — and found the house arranged like a patient's chart: clear passages, nothing out of place, every room labelled by function and nothing more.

Stairwells at both ends. A service door half-open near the kitchen wing, and through it the sound of a knife on a board.

Lisette came up the back stairs with a basket of linens against her hip and stopped at the sight of him, rearranging her grip. She waited, expression unchanged, for him to speak first.

She gathered the basket back up. "The ones who'd remember would be Dr. Osei and the women who run the school. They'll tell you, if they think it's worth telling you. Ask them the same question you just asked me and watch their faces."

She started up the stair, then paused and looked down at him over the banister. "And there's a man who keeps the chandler's on the eastern road, Bellamy. Bernard used to stop in and buy candles he had no need of. He'd have heard every promise made in that quarter for thirty years."

Julian tipped his head back to catch her eye over the banister. "Bellamy. Candles he had no need of." A faint, wry note crept in. "Your grandfather knew what he was doing. Bernard, I mean."

He turned back toward the corridor. "Quieter clothes, then a ride east. Send word ahead if you can — I'd rather Dr. Osei hear I'm coming from someone other than a footman in a good coat." He paused. "And Lisette — the room Bernard kept for himself. I'll be wanting it. It's his house I'm here to walk through, not a guest's."

[#1357 Narration]
Lisette's chin dipped in something close to approval, though her expression stayed flat as a closed door. "I'll see the room's ready before you're back. The linens have been shut up in the cupboard eight weeks, they'll want airing."

She adjusted her grip on the basket. "As for the doctor — I'll send word through the kitchen, not the front hall. The eastern quarter trusts a cook's boy faster than a footman." A beat. "Anything else you need doing, I'll be about the house."

"Then I'll leave it in your hands." Julian gave her a last nod and turned back down the corridor, boots quiet on the runner. His jaw was set now, not tense but decided.

He crossed to the bay and ran a hand along its neck while he waited, scratching under the mane the way he'd been taught as a boy, back before any of this. It was an old, steady gesture, and his shoulders came down a notch with it.

[#1368 Julian]

Bellamy picked up the tin again and turned it in his hands, not sorting anymore, just holding it.

"But he's had twelve years to decide what a Redmist promise is worth, and one more offer from the family name won't move him on its own. "First stone already paid for, then. Not offered." Julian nodded slowly, the shape of it settling. "I'll want a mason's name and a figure before I ride to the clinic — a real one, not a number I carry in my head. You've watched this quarter thirty years. He reached into his coat and laid a hand flat on the counter, palm up. "And Bellamy — if I pay for that wing, I'd sooner it went up with your name somewhere on the contract than some firm from across the harbour. You've no reason to do me a kindness, but I'm asking anyway."

[#1373 Narration]
Bellamy weighed that for a long moment, his mouth working as though the notion were a wick he had to thread before he could trust it.

He lifted his hand from the tin and let it hover there between them, an old calloused palm. "And I'll put my name to it. Not for kindness. He clasped Julian's hand.

[#1374 Julian]
Bellamy's grip was dry and hard, and Julian held it a beat longer than a formality.

"Then Tull it is. And when the wing goes up, I'll see you're there for the laying of the first stone — you and Dr. Osei both, since the two of you can argue over who gets the credit." He let go and straightened. "One more thing before I take up your morning. You knew Bernard as well as anyone down here. If you had to say it plain — what was he, in your book? Not the charities, not the name. The man who bought candles he didn't need."

He asked it evenly, not softening it, and waited.

[#1375 Narration]
Bellamy let go of the tin and rested both hands flat on the counter, looking at Julian as though the answer had to be dug out from someplace deep and wasn't going to come up clean.

"Bernard was a man who wanted to be better than he was, and couldn't quite manage it, and knew it." He said it without malice. "The candles were his way of paying a debt he couldn't name. He'd stand in this shop and talk about the wing, and I'd listen, and we both knew he'd go home and buy a hospital someplace the name would show." A shrug. "Not a bad man. A tired one. There's a difference, and it cost this quarter plenty."

He picked up the tin again, and this time the wicks went back under his fingers. "Tull's shop is the one with the red door. Tell him I sent you and he'll charge you fair and grumble the whole way through."

The door opened a crack, then wider. The man behind it was built like a barrel and grey with stone dust from shoulder to boots, a mallet still in one fist.

"Shop's closed to callers," he said, and started to shut it.

From behind him, across the yard, a second voice carried — reedy, aggrieved. "It's the Redmist party, you great fool. Let them in before you cost me the job."

The door swung open the rest of the way.

[#1380 Julian]
Julian stepped in past the barrel-chested man without ceremony, dust and all.

"Bellamy sent me. Tull's expecting me — or he will be, once he hears why." He let his eyes move over the yard, the mallet, the stone chips scattered across the ground. "I'm told you're slow as wet paint and twice as honest. I'm here about the clinic's east wing. So tell me what a real one would cost, and don't pretty it up on my account."

[#1381 Narration]
Tull came around the yard's edge, a wiry man in his sixties with raw knuckles and a mason's apron stiff with old lime. He looked Julian over, then the door, then the barrel-chested man, who had the sense to step back and find something to do with his mallet.

"Bellamy sent you, so I'll hear the words." Tull wiped his hands on the apron. "East wing. Brick or stone? Because if you want stone, I've a quarry that's owed me a delivery since spring, and that comes with a price in temper if not in coin." He squinted. "And what's the clinic now, so I don't build a wing onto a ruin."

[#1382 Julian]
"Stone, if the quarry can be trusted to deliver it. Brick if it can't — I'd rather have a wing than a feud with a quarryman." Julian stepped further into the yard, turning to take in the stone chips and the mallet work. "The clinic's still standing. It's the only surgery on that side of the harbour and it's been running on the doctor's goodwill and unpaid overtime. What you'd be building onto is sound enough, but it's not much bigger than this yard, so mind your figures on scale."

He nodded toward Tull's apron. "How long would you want? The temporary rooms Bernard paid for are twelve years old now. I'm not looking to rush you into a bad wall, but these people have waited long enough."

[#1383 Narration]
Tull crouched to the stone chips at his feet, weighing one between two fingers while he chewed over the answer.

"Stone, then. My quarryman's owed me a favour and I'll collect it in his own yard if he doesn't deliver." He dropped the chip. "Six months for the shell and the roof, longer for the fittings if Osei wants plumbing that doesn't freeze. You'll have the figure in writing by tomorrow, with the quarry's price on a separate line so you can see what I'm not skimming." He straightened and met Julian's eye. "'Til then, the first stone stands paid the moment I've a contract and the drayman's first load ordered. That's how I'd put it to Osei."

[#1384 Julian]
"Six months for the shell and the roof." Julian looked up at the yard walls as though measuring them against a building he hadn't seen yet. "I'll have your figure in writing by tomorrow, and I'll want the quarry's line itemised like you said, so Dr. Osei can see it's not padded on his account."

He pulled on his gloves and turned back toward the door. "One last thing. When the contract's drawn up, I'll want the first stone laid with Bellamy and Osei both standing to see it. You've built in this quarter long enough to know what that means better than I do, so tell me plain — will that make things easier with the men you'd hire, or harder?"

[#1385 Narration]
Tull rubbed the back of his neck, leaving a smear of lime dust across the skin.

"Easier. The men in this quarter won't take a job on a stranger's word, but they'll take one on mine, and Bellamy standing at the laying tells them the money's real and the old man's handshake has finally come good." He picked up his mallet and set it against the wall. "Harder only in one way. When you lay a first stone in front of witnesses, you can't quietly walk away after. Word gets around. It'll be the measure they hold you to."

[#1386 Julian]
Julian nodded slowly. "Then let it get around. I'd rather be held to it in the street than trusted on paper." He pulled the door open and stepped back out into the lane. "Tomorrow, then. Send your figure to the estate — Jezebel's the one with the folder, and I'll see it before the day's out."

He swung back up onto the bay. Once they were riding, he leaned toward Carla. "One more stop. Six months for a shell and a roof means Osei's been told a dozen versions of this. If I walk in and hand him Tull's name first, before he's had a chance to decide I'm another coat with a smoother promise, it might buy me the corridor."

He glanced at her. "When we get there, I want you to watch the door and the street, like before. But I want you to tell me plain afterward — did the man believe me, or did he only hear me out?"

[#1387 Narration]
Carla clicked her tongue and the jenny stepped off the gravel into the lane.

"Watching a man's face while he decides whether to believe you — I'll manage. Just don't make it hard for me." A glance sideways. "If he asks a question you haven't got an answer for, let the silence sit. Men fill silence with the truth more often than not, and Osei's been waiting twelve years for an excuse to say his piece."

The harbour road bent east along the water, past net-menders and a fish shed where a boy was hacking ice into a barrow, then turned inland up a lane where the houses stood shoulder to shoulder and the gutters ran with soapy water. The clinic had a painted board over the door — the letters worn but legible — and a row of people waiting on a bench outside it, bundled into coats, one of them holding a child against her shoulder.

[#1388 Julian]
Julian reined the bay in a little way down the lane and sat a moment, looking at the bench and the people on it. Then he dismounted, handed the reins to Carla without a word, and walked up to the clinic door at an unhurried pace — not past the waiting row, but along it, meeting eyes where they were offered.

He stopped at the doorway and put his head inside. "Dr. Osei? I'm Julian Redmist. I know you were told to expect someone today. I've come from Tull the mason's yard, and I'd rather say the rest of it to you directly than through a door."

[#1389 Narration]
The boy on the bench twisted round to look at Julian, and the woman with the child pulled her coat a little closer. He glanced past Julian to the bay, the grey-coated woman holding both sets of reins, and something in his shoulders shifted — not softened, but braced. "Tull's yard, was it. "I'll tell you straight, since you've had twelve years of being told things slantwise. Bernard promised this clinic an east wing. He shook on it. Then he bought temporary rooms instead, and I've just come from the chandler's shop where I learned exactly what that cost you."

He let the silence sit a moment, as Carla had said.

"I'm not here to say the old man was misunderstood. I'm here because Tull's promised me six months for the shell and roof, Bellamy's putting his name to the first stone, and the quarry's price will be on the contract in plain figures where you can see it. [#1391 Narration]
Osei folded the cloth and set it down with deliberate care, which gave him time to arrange his face.

"Twelve years." He took his spectacles off entirely and polished them on his sleeve. "Twelve years, and the answer's still a wing, but I'd be lying if I said the same wing. Fevers don't kill the way they did when Bernard stood in this room. What kills now is the harbour — crushed hands, bad ropes, men who wait two days before they come in because they can't afford the time off." He set the spectacles back on his nose. "What I need is a room I can cut in. Proper light, a floor that drains, enough space that I'm not working around a woman in labour. If Tull can build that, I'll take his wing and shake his hand."

He paused. "There'll be one more thing, and I'll say it now rather than later. The men who work this door — I want one of them trained. Not by me, I've no gift for teaching. But if the family's paying for a building, I'm asking it to pay for a lad who can hold a needle steady when I'm not here."

[#1392 Julian]

"A room you can cut in. Proper light, a floor that drains." He turned back. "That's a different wing than the one Tull priced. That's the price of the family's money and it seems a fair one. But it shouldn't come out of the building fund, so I'd know what paying for it looks like. Is that a wage for an apprentice while he learns, or a fee to whoever takes him on? Name it plain and I'll carry it back to Jezebel with everything else."

[#1393 Narration]
Osei leaned back against the edge of his examination table, arms folded, giving the question its due.

"A wage, and a small one. The lad works the door and the dressings while he learns, so he earns most of what I'd pay him. Whoever takes him on for the cutting — and I've a surgeon in mind across the water, she's agreed to it if the money's there — she'd want her fee paid direct, no haggling through me." He unpinned his spectacles and folded them. "I'll put both figures on paper tonight and send them to the estate with Tull's."

His eyes came back to Julian. "The old plan. I still have it, drawn up and put away. If Tull's going to build a cutting room, he'll want to see what he's been asked to improve on."

[#1394 Julian]
"Then it's settled. Old plan in Tull's hands by tomorrow, figures to the estate with it, and the cutting room drawn up fresh instead of borrowed." Julian pulled his coat straight. "I'll not keep your patients waiting any longer than I already have."

He got as far as the door, then turned back, one hand on the frame. "Dr. Osei — the lad you train. Ten years from now, if he's standing where you are, cut in better than any of it, I'll consider that wing well spent. See it's a good one."

[#1395 Narration]
Osei's mouth twitched at the corner, which on a man like him amounted to a broad grin.

"A good one," he said, and pulled the door open for Julian himself. "I'll hold you to that, and so will the lane. Word travels faster down here than any runner your clerk can send."

[#1396 Julian]
Julian stepped off the clinic's worn step and walked back along the bench, slowing as he came to the woman with the child.

"Doctor's still seeing folk," he said, keeping his voice low. "I've held the door long enough — I'll not hold the queue too."

He crossed to the bay and took the reins from Carla. Before mounting, he glanced up at her, quiet enough that the bench wouldn't hear. "You watched. Did he believe me, or did he only hear me out?"

[#1397 Narration]
Carla swung up into the jenny's saddle before she answered, and the mare turned a slow circle in the lane while she settled the reins.

"Believed you." She pulled alongside, her voice pitched for the two of them. "When you said the lad should be a good one, he near smiled. A man who's humouring you doesn't smile at that." She glanced down the lane. "He'll put his figures on paper and he'll mean them, and if the building's late he'll be down at Tull's yard being difficult about it. Which is exactly what you want."

The jenny stepped out toward the harbour road. "Osei's the easy part, mind. A man who wanted what you offered was always going to take it. The cousins won't be."

[#1398 Julian]
Julian mounted and turned the bay back up the lane, letting it walk until the bench and the clinic door had fallen behind them.

"The cousins, then." He gathered the reins. "You said there were letters. I read them this morning before I came out — three of them, and not one of them says what it wants in plain words. It's all 'the integrity of the family line' and 'our grandfather's true intention.'" He glanced at Carla. "I've a mind to answer them the same way Osei answers a fever. Straight to the source, no guessing what's underneath it. But I'd hear your read on it first, since you were on that side of the desk before you were on mine. What do the cousins actually want. Money, or the house, or just the satisfaction of having been right about me?"

[#1399 Narration]
Carla rode a while before answering, her eyes on the road ahead.

"Money, mostly. One of them — the elder, Alistair — he's got debts he's spent years hiding, and a will like that is the first break in the wall. The other two will tell themselves it's principle." She turned the jenny around a drain grate. "None of them want the house. None of them want you. She glanced across. "Answer them straight and they'll read it as a weakness. Men chasing a settlement smell eagerness the way dogs smell fear."

[#1400 Julian]
Julian rode in silence for a stretch of the harbour road, the bay's hooves finding their own rhythm while he turned her words over.

"Then they don't get a straight answer that reads like eagerness. They get a straight answer that reads like a bill." He looked across at her. "Alistair's debts — how much trouble is he actually in? Because if he's desperate, he'll take a settlement and call it justice. If he's comfortable, he'll drag this out for years and the clinic pays for it."

He turned the bay toward the estate lane. "And here's what I'll not do. I'll not have the foundations' money sitting in escrow while three cousins thrash it out in a courtroom. If they want their cut, they can have it named and paid, once, on paper, in return for a signed withdrawal of the claim. No open-ended fight." He paused. "Tell me if that's a fool's idea before I say it to Jezebel."

"Then I'll see Jezebel before I write anything. If the foundations can't carry the escrow without the clinic feeling it, then the cousins wait, and they wait loudly, and I'll let them." He scraped the mud from his boots at the side door. "A settlement's only worth what it buys, and if it buys the clinic a lean year, it's not worth having."

Inside, the corridor was cooler than the yard and the afternoon sun lay in long bars across the marble. He nodded toward the library. "Come with me. I'd have you in the room when I put it to her — if she says the escrow's fine, I want to hear it twice, and if she says it isn't, I want to know if she's guessing."

[#1403 Narration]
Jezebel was at the desk by the window, the leather folder open and a second ledger beside it, a cup of tea gone cold at her elbow. She looked up as the door swung, and her pen came to rest.

"Back from the eastern quarter, and still breathing. That's encouraging." She took in Julian's coat, then Carla standing by the shelves with her cap in her hands, and her eyes narrowed slightly. "You've that look about you. Sit down and tell me what I'm about to have to find money for."

She turned the ledger around, sliding it across the desk toward him with a thumb still marking the page.

[#1404 Julian]
Julian pulled out the chair and sat, but didn't take up the ledger yet. "The clinic needs a cutting room, not just the wing Bernard sketched twelve years ago. Tull's costing it fresh, and there's an apprentice surgeon's wage and a teaching fee on top of that. Dr. Osei's sending the figures to you by tomorrow." He leaned forward. "But before any of that — the cousins. I want to end them with a settlement, paid once, on paper, for a signed withdrawal of the claim. Which means I need to know whether the foundations can carry that escrow without the clinic feeling a lean year."

[#1405 Narration]
Jezebel drew the ledger back toward herself, turned it around, and ran a finger down a column before speaking.

"The foundations can carry an escrow. Not a generous one." She tapped a figure near the bottom. "That's what's liquid by month's end. Set a settlement against it and the clinic still gets paid, the school still gets paid, but the cushions are gone. If a roof falls in somewhere this year, we come to you with a hat in our hands."

She closed the ledger and looked at him plainly. "So the question isn't whether the money's there. It's what number you're willing to put to Alistair, and I'd want to hear it before his solicitor hears anything."

[#1406 Julian]
Julian pulled the ledger a little closer and read the figure near the bottom twice before he answered.

"Then the number has to come in under that line, or it's not a settlement, it's a wound I'm opening myself." He turned the ledger back around. "I want Alistair's debts looked into before I name anything. If the moneylender off Collier's Row is the real pressure, then I want to know what he owes to the week before I decide whether I'm paying off a debt or paying off a man." He glanced at Jezebel. "Can that be done quietly? Because if Alistair finds out I've been asking, he'll raise the figure out of spite alone."

[#1407 Narration]
Jezebel straightened a stack of papers that didn't need straightening.

"Quietly is the only way I'd do it. "But I'll not ask him to dig into Alistair's private affairs until I know what I'll do with what he finds. If Alistair owes the Row three hundred in the week, do I pay it and hand him the rest, or do I pay only the Row and make him take a smaller sum to his creditors?"

She looked up. "That's your decision, not mine. But it decides the number before my man ever sets foot on that street."

[#1408 Julian]
Julian frowned at the ledger, weighing it out loud rather than to the room.

"Pay only the Row and let him carry the rest to his creditors, and he'll take it because he's got no choice — but he'll hate me for it, and a man who hates me with a signed withdrawal in his pocket is a man who'll find a lawyer with a keener eye." He looked up at Jezebel. "Pay the Row, hand him a smaller sum to see to his own affairs, and put a condition on it. [#1409 Narration]
Jezebel drew the ledger back and closed it, weighing the shape of what he'd said.

"There's something else you should hear from me rather than the board. The will's been read, but it's not yet been proved. But if Alistair lodges a caveat before the seal's on it, everything stops where it stands — the clinic, Tull, all of it. [#1410 Julian]
Julian let out a slow breath and looked at the cold tea, the closed ledger, the papers on Bernard's desk that nobody had cleared.

"Before probate. So I've got a clock on it and I didn't know." He straightened in the chair. "Then here's what I'll do, and you tell me if it's too fast. I write to Alistair tomorrow — not a settlement offer, just a letter that says I've read his and I'd rather settle this between us than in a courtroom. He pushed the ledger back across the desk. "But I'll not write it tonight. She gathered her papers into the folder. "But I'd not stake the clinic on his solicitor being slow. The kitchen was all brick and steam, a great iron range on one wall and a scrubbed table with flour on it. Louise stood over a cutting board, her black undercut pinned back, sleeves rolled, a knife working through herbs at a speed that suggested feelings. "You're the one who's been in the house since yesterday and hadn't the decency to send word about breakfast."

[#1414 Julian]
Julian crossed the kitchen and stopped at the end of the scrubbed table, well short of the cutting board.

"You've had a day's notice, so I won't pretend I'm some mystery. Eggs hard, tea strong, and beyond that I'll eat what's in front of me and tell you honest whether it's any good." He nodded at the herbs under her knife. "I'd have sent word sooner, but I spent the morning finding out my grandfather promised people things he never delivered. [#1415 Narration]
Louise turned the knife flat side down and swept the herbs into a waiting bowl in one motion.

"Beef bourguignon, and don't look stricken, I'd already started it before I heard." She nodded toward the range, where a heavy pot sat with something dark and patient inside. "The estate had a cellar beef that needed using, and if I'd waited a day for word from you, it would have spoiled. You'll get it tonight or nobody will."

She wiped her hands on her apron and looked him over properly for the first time, her yellow eyes steady.

"Hard eggs and strong tea, then. That's a breakfast that doesn't trust anyone." A pause. "Did you really spend the morning finding out your grandfather broke promises, or is that something you say to excuse not sending a note?"

[#1416 Julian]
"No, it's not an excuse." Julian rested his hands flat on the scrubbed table. "I went down to the eastern quarter this morning because my grandfather shook hands on a wing for the clinic twelve years ago and never built it. He straightened. "And I'd rather not add to the list of promises this house makes and forgets. So yes, I should have sent a note about eggs. But I meant what I said after it, too."

Louise held his eyes a moment longer than was comfortable, then picked up her knife again.

"The bourguignon will be ready at seven," she said. "And I'll expect an honest word on it. Not polite. Honest."

[#1417 Narration]
Louise said it the way a challenge gets laid down, and then she turned back to her board and the matter was closed. "Seven," she repeated, without looking up. "I'll have the bread out at six-forty-five. If you're late, I'll not hold it warm for you."

The knife resumed its rhythm. A pot on the range gave a soft, thick sound — the bourguignon finding its temper — and she leaned to adjust the flame with a flick of her wrist.

"You'll want to wash up before then. There's flour in the corridor that's got a bootprint in it and I'd guess the boot was yours."

[#1418 Julian]
Julian glanced down at the flour-dusted print his boot had left near the threshold, and had the grace to look abashed.

"Fair enough. I'll sweep that up on my way out and mind where my feet go the next time I come through a working kitchen." He tapped the table once, lightly. "Seven o'clock. Bread at quarter to. I'll be washed and honest."

He turned for the service stair, then paused at the door, one hand on the frame. "Louise — the beef's a good use of a cellar that would have spoiled. That's the kind of thinking I'd like this house to run on. Not instructions passed down and obeyed. Sense."

[#1419 Narration]
Louise's knife paused on the board again. When she looked up this time, the challenge in her face had eased into something more thoughtful.

"Not instructions passed down and obeyed." She tried the notion out, and her shoulders made a small, wry movement. "You'll find no argument here. The last head chef could not be told anything — not by me, not by the fishmonger. We ate badly for a year."

Her attention returned to the herbs, but the rhythm now was brisk rather than sharp, easy in the wrist. "Go and wash, then. You'll find the print by the door wants the broom, and the broom is in the cupboard to your left."

[#1420 Julian]
Julian found the broom in the cupboard to his left and swept the flour back into a neat line against the threshold, then carried the dust to the bin and knocked it out.

"Broom's where you said," he called back over his shoulder, returning it to the cupboard. "And the floor's better for it. If the last head chef couldn't be told anything, I'd guess the kitchen's been wanting for sense longer than a year."

He washed at the sink and dried his hands, then turned back toward her.

"Since I've time before seven — you trained under your mother, by your own account. What did she cook that you still can't get right? Because I've found there's always one dish a person can't get right, and it tells you more about them than anything they've mastered."

[#1421 Narration]
Louise set the knife down entirely and leaned her hip against the counter, giving the question the respect of a real answer.

"Sole meunière." She said it like a confession. "My mother made it with her eyes closed. Butter, lemon, capers, flour fine as dust. "It is the flour. I know it is the flour. But her flour came from a miller two streets from our restaurant and it is not the same flour, and so it is not the same dish, and I have decided to hate it rather than admit that."

A beat. "What about you, then. What is yours?"

[#1422 Julian]
Julian set the towel down folded on the edge of the sink.

"Rice pudding." He said it without any shame at all. "My mother made it whenever the week had been a hard one. Rice, milk, a bit of sugar, and she'd stand over it the whole time so it didn't catch. I've made it a hundred times and it's never once been hers. Mine's either soup or glue and never anything in between, and I've decided the milk in this city is wrong rather than admit I'm scared of a burnt pan."

He pushed away from the sink. "So we're a pair. Your flour and my milk. If the bourguignon's any good at seven, I'll tell you honest, and if you ever want a second opinion on which miller's flour is closest to your mother's, I'd ride out with you to find him. But I'll not eat sole meunière to judge it, because I've never had a good one and I'd only be guessing."

Julian sat down at the far end of the table, drew the bowl close, and broke off a piece of bread. He spooned up a piece of the beef with a little of the dark sauce clinging to it, blew on it once, and ate.

He chewed slowly, paying attention. Then he looked up at her, still chewing, and pointed the spoon at the bowl.

"You said it's better tomorrow." He swallowed. "I'll want to know what tomorrow tastes like, because if this is it being modest, I've been eating badly my whole life and didn't know it." Louise let out a breath through her nose, something settling in her shoulders as she heard it.

"Good," she said, and the word came out plain, all the pushiness gone out of it. She took her own bowl to the table and sat down across from him, which she hadn't done for the head chef in a year. "Tomorrow it will be deeper. The wine goes quiet overnight and the beef remembers it was a working animal." She tore a piece of bread. "You eat without talking about the accounts. I had thought the new owner would want figures on the table by the second bite."

She ate a spoonful herself, watching him over the rim. "Hard eggs and strong tea. Is that all you ask of a morning, or is there something you have not thought to ask for because nobody has offered?"

Julian set his spoon down and gave the question real thought instead of reaching for the first answer.

"Nobody's offered me much of anything in a while, so I'd have to dig for it." He tore the bread smaller than he needed to. "My mother made a thing called a bread-and-butter pudding when money was thin and the bread had gone stale. It was never a treat, exactly. It was what we had. But she'd put a bit of lemon peel in it and it came out better than anything the baker's shop sold." He looked up. "That's honest. "On the good nights, my father would shut the restaurant early and we would eat in the kitchen with the door locked — no customers, no menu." She turned her bread over. She looked up, and her yellow eyes had a considering quality. "Bread-and-butter pudding with lemon peel. That is two nights from now — I will need the bread to go stale on purpose, which will annoy the baker. And you will tell me honest whether it is your mother's or only mine."
